Socrates, one of the most influential philosophers of antiquity, employed a unique method of inquiry now known as the Socratic method. He never wrote any philosophical texts himself; our knowledge of him comes primarily from the dialogues of his student, Plato. In these dialogues, Socrates is depicted as a man of great intellectual humility, famously claiming that the only thing he knew was that he knew nothing. The Socratic method is a form of cooperative argumentative dialogue between individuals, based on asking and answering questions to stimulate critical thinking and to draw out ideas and underlying presumptions. Socrates would engage in conversation with someone who claimed to have expertise in a certain area, such as justice or courage. Through a series of probing questions, he would reveal the contradictions and flaws in their thinking, leading them to a state of 'aporia', or intellectual confusion. This was not done to humiliate, but to clear the ground of false beliefs, allowing for a more rigorous and genuine search for truth. This method was a stark contrast to the Sophists of his time, who were itinerant teachers that charged fees for instruction in rhetoric and virtue, often teaching how to win an argument regardless of the truth. Socrates sought truth, not victory, and he never charged for his teaching, which ultimately contributed to his trial and execution on charges of impiety and corrupting the youth of Athens. Q- What was the ultimate goal of the Socratic method?

questions.questionHtml: Which part of the human eye is responsible for controlling the amount of light entering the eye?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is the Iris.

Explanation:

The iris is the colored, muscular part of the eye that functions as a diaphragm. It controls the amount of light entering the eye by adjusting the size of the pupil.

This automatic process is known as the pupillary light reflex. While the pupil is the actual opening through which light passes, it's the iris's muscle movements that regulate its size.

The other parts have different functions:

Confusing Point: Pupil or Iris?

The pupil is the black circular opening in the center of the eye through which light enters. It’s just a hole — it doesn’t have any muscles or power to control light by itself.

The iris, on the other hand, is the colored part of the eye (brown, blue, green, etc.) that surrounds the pupil. It is made up of muscles that can expand or contract the pupil depending on the amount of light.
